routes.name: Northeast Ridge
routes.best_season: Midsummer to early fall, once the steep gully to the saddle and the west-side ledges are free of snow. Summer afternoons bring frequent lightning, so aim for an early summit.
routes.overview: The standard route on Pyramid Peak climbs from Maroon Lake into the amphitheater under the north face, up a steep scree slope to a saddle on the northeast ridge, then weaves across exposed ledges and gullies to the summit. It is one of the most serious standard routes on a Colorado fourteener: short on distance but sustained, exposed and built of notoriously loose rock. Expect constant route-finding and real consequences for a slip or a dropped rock.
routes.beta: From the saddle at about 13,000 ft, follow the ridge crest and ledges on its right side. Near 13,300 ft the route crosses a small gap in the ridge, the "leap of faith" - a short step across rather than a true leap - onto narrow, exposed ledges beyond. Around 13,400 ft you reach a steep band of greenish rock (the "green wall"); climb it on Class 3-4 ledges, testing every hold. Above, the route works up a series of gullies and ledges on the west side of the ridge, marked by cairns; staying on the cairned line keeps the difficulty at Class 3-4, while wandering usually lands you on steeper, looser ground. Above about 13,900 ft the angle eases and you walk to the summit. Note landmarks on the way up, because the upper route is easy to lose on the way down.
routes.approach: From Maroon Lake Trailhead, take the Crater Lake trail about 1.5 miles to a junction near 10,100 ft and turn left onto the Pyramid Peak trail. It climbs steeply through forest to the entrance of the amphitheater below Pyramid's north face at about 11,200 ft, where the maintained trail ends. Cross the rock glacier in the amphitheater on a faint, cairned path, then climb the steep scree and dirt slope, roughly 1,000 ft of gain, to the saddle on the northeast ridge at about 13,000 ft.
routes.descent_text: Descend the same route, reversing the ledges, gullies, green wall and ridge gap back to the saddle, then down the steep scree slope to the amphitheater. Go slowly: the loose terrain is more dangerous going down, and the cairned line is easy to miss from above.
routes.turnaround: Turn around if you are not on the summit by late morning or if storms are building; the exposed ridge and ledges offer no shelter and are slow to retreat across. Also turn back if you lose the cairned line and find yourself on terrain harder than Class 4.
routes.bail: Above the saddle the only practical retreat is back the way you came; the gullies off the ridge are loose and cliffed out. Below the saddle, the scree slope back to the amphitheater is the escape to the trail.

pitch_detail.notes: Crater Lake trail, then the steep Pyramid Peak trail through forest to about 11,200 ft.
Cross the rock glacier on a faint cairned path below the north face.
Steep scree and dirt, about 1,000 ft of gain to the northeast ridge saddle near 13,000 ft; rockfall from parties above.
Ledges on and right of the crest; step across a small gap near 13,300 ft onto narrow, exposed ledges.
Steep band of greenish rock near 13,400 ft; loose holds, test everything.
Follow cairns through gullies and ledges on the west side of the ridge; staying on route keeps it at Class 3-4.
Above about 13,900 ft the angle eases to the summit.

gear: Sturdy approach shoes or light boots with good edging
what_to_bring: Plenty of water - little reliable water above the amphitheater
Gloves for scrambling on rough rock
obj_haz: Frequent rockfall from climbers above and from the north face
Loose, fractured rock on nearly every hold
Exposed ledges where a slip would be fatal
Afternoon thunderstorms with no shelter on the ridge
Snow in the gully to the saddle early in the season
routes.watch_out:
Do not climb directly below another party on the scree slope or in the gullies
Losing the cairned line quickly leads onto steeper, looser ground
The route is harder to follow on the way down than on the way up
Test every handhold - large blocks can be loose
pro_tips: Wear a helmet from the amphitheater up
Start before dawn to be off the ridge before afternoon storms
Look back often on the ascent to memorize the descent line
Keep your party close together in gullies so a dislodged rock cannot gain speed
If you knock a rock loose, shout "rock" immediately

road.name: Maroon Creek Road
road.driveNote: Drive from Aspen up Maroon Creek Road to Maroon Lake. From late May to mid-October, private vehicles may not drive in between 8:00 AM and 5:00 PM; the rest of the day, driving in requires a paid parking reservation (day, midnight-to-midnight, evening or overnight). For a pre-dawn start, reserve parking and arrive before 8:00 AM. During restricted hours, access is by the paid shuttle from Aspen Highlands, which also needs an advance reservation and starts too late for a climb of this length. Outside the shuttle season the road may be closed to cars by snow.

timing.recommendedStart: Before dawn, aiming to summit by late morning

access.land_manager: White River National Forest - Maroon Bells-Snowmass Wilderness
access.permit: No advance wilderness permit for a day climb. Paid parking or shuttle reservation required to reach Maroon Lake in season. Camping at Crater Lake needs an advance overnight permit; overnight trips elsewhere self-register at the trailhead. Group size limit 10.
access.fees: Parking reservation $10 per vehicle; shuttle $16 per adult ($10 seniors and children)

routes.name: Southwest Ridge
routes.rock_grade: Exposed Class 3 ledges and ridge scrambling
routes.best_season: Mid-July through September, once the snow is off the ridge and Big Bear Creek on the approach road has dropped. Afternoon thunderstorms are routine in July and August, so plan to be off the ridge by midday.
routes.overview: The standard route up Wilson Peak, a steep, striking fourteener in the San Miguel Mountains west of Telluride. A long trail climbs through old mining country in Silver Pick Basin to the Rock of Ages saddle, then a short, exposed Class 3 ridge leads over a false summit and through a notch to the top. The approach is gentle, but the final ridge is serious scrambling with real exposure.
routes.beta: From the Rock of Ages saddle, head east across a loose, rugged slope to the small saddle between Wilson Peak and Gladstone Peak. From there, traverse the south side of the ridge on Class 3 ledges and climb up to the southwest ridge at around 13,550 ft. Follow the ridge, mostly on a faint path just right of the crest, to a false summit at about 13,900 ft. From the false summit, downclimb roughly 50 ft into a notch, then scramble across stacked blocks and ledges through a prominent gash in the ridge and make the final exposed Class 3 moves to the summit. Take your time on the downclimb; it is the most exposed part of the route and is harder to reverse on the way back.
routes.approach: From the Rock of Ages Trailhead, follow the Wilson Mesa Trail for about half a mile to the start of the Rock of Ages Trail. The trail climbs gradually out of Elk Creek Basin into Silver Pick Basin, following old mining roads past historic mine ruins and a cabin, then switchbacks up talus slopes to the Rock of Ages saddle, about 4 miles from the trailhead. The trail crosses private land on an easement in Silver Pick Basin, so stay on the trail. The mine ruins and cabin are private property and not open to visitors.
routes.descent_text: Descend the way you came: reverse the ridge, including the climb back up out of the notch to the false summit, then retrace the Class 3 ledges to the Wilson Peak–Gladstone saddle, cross back to the Rock of Ages saddle, and follow the trail down to the trailhead.
routes.turnaround: Set a firm turnaround time for the summit and turn back if thunderstorms are building. Do not start the ridge if the ledges are wet, icy or snow-covered.
routes.bail: Before the ridge, bail by returning from either saddle to the Rock of Ages Trail. On the ridge, the only safe exit is reversing the route; the faces off the ridge are steep and loose.

pitch_detail.pitch: Trailhead to Rock of Ages saddle
pitch_detail.notes: About 4 miles on the Wilson Mesa and Rock of Ages trails through Silver Pick Basin; talus switchbacks near the top. Stay on the trail across private land.

pitch_detail.pitch: Rock of Ages saddle to Wilson–Gladstone saddle
pitch_detail.notes: Cross a loose, rugged slope east to the small saddle between Wilson Peak and Gladstone Peak.
Traverse ledges on the south side and climb up onto the southwest ridge around 13,550 ft.
Follow the ridge, mostly on a faint path right of the crest, to the false summit at about 13,900 ft.
Downclimb about 50 ft into the notch, scramble across stacked blocks and ledges through the gash, then make the final exposed moves to the summit.

what_to_bring: Plenty of water (none at the trailhead)
hazards: Exposure on the ridge and notch
Lingering snow early in the season
routes.watch_out:
The downclimb into the notch below the false summit is the crux and is exposed
The false summit is not the top
Stay on the trail through Silver Pick Basin; the mine ruins and cabin are private
Big Bear Creek on the approach road can be too deep for low-clearance cars early in the season
pro_tips: Start before dawn so you are off the ridge before storms build
Wear a helmet, especially if other parties are on the ridge
Keep to the faint path just right of the crest; it avoids much of the loose rock
Low-clearance cars can park at the pullout before the Big Bear Creek crossing and walk the last stretch of road

road.name: Silver Pick Road (County Road 60M) to Forest Road 622 and Forest Road 645
road.status: Open in summer; rough dirt road
road.driveNote: From Highway 145 west of Telluride, take Silver Pick Road (County Road 60M) south to the forest boundary, continue on Forest Road 622 to the Wilson Mesa Trailhead, then follow Forest Road 645 to the Rock of Ages Trailhead. The road is rough with deep ruts in places, and FR 645 fords Big Bear Creek, which is usually manageable by mid-July. High clearance is recommended, with 4WD preferred. Low-clearance cars can park at a small pullout before the creek, about 1.2 miles short of the trailhead.

access.land_manager: US Forest Service, Grand Mesa, Uncompahgre and Gunnison National Forests (Lizard Head Wilderness), with a trail easement across private land in Silver Pick Basin
access.permit: None required. The route was closed in 2004 when landowners in Silver Pick Basin shut the traditional path to the summit ridge. Public access was restored in stages: key land on the southwest ridge was bought and transferred to the Forest Service in 2007, the Rock of Ages Trail was built on public land, and a trail easement across the remaining private parcel in the upper basin was secured in 2011. The route is open to the public today, but it still crosses private land, so stay on the trail. Horses are not allowed on the private section, and camping is not allowed at the trailhead. Wilderness rules on party size, camping and campfires apply.

routes.name: Arapaho Peaks Traverse
routes.rock_grade: Class 3 ridge with a short Class 4 crux
routes.best_season: Mid-July through mid-September, once the snow has melted off the ridge and the trailhead road is open. Summer afternoons bring frequent thunderstorms, so start early.
routes.overview: A classic ridge scramble linking the two Arapaho Peaks, finishing on North Arapaho, the highest summit in the Indian Peaks. A good trail leads to South Arapaho, then a sustained, exposed Class 3 ridge with a brief Class 4 crux leads north above the Arapaho Glacier. Most parties return the same way, back over South Arapaho.
routes.beta: Trail to South Arapaho: follow the Arapaho Pass trail to the Fourth of July Mine ruins, then switch back northeast on the signed Arapaho Glacier trail. It climbs steadily above treeline to the saddle southeast of South Arapaho, where the trail ends and a rocky, loose Class 2 scramble past a false summit leads to the top. The traverse: from South Arapaho's summit, follow the connecting ridge north, about three quarters of a mile one way. Almost all of it is Class 3, with roughly 300 ft of downclimbing and 400 ft of climbing each way, including a somewhat exposed Class 3 downclimb of about 50 ft early on. Stay near the crest and escape to the west side at difficulties; the east side drops to the glacier. Occasional painted marks and cairns show the line but are sparse. The crux: about three quarters of the way to North Arapaho, two short steps of roughly 8-10 ft each go at Class 4 on good holds; some parties find a line that stays Class 3. Final slopes: easier ground, sometimes with a lingering snow patch, leads to North Arapaho's broad summit. Allow at least an hour each way on the ridge.
routes.approach: From the Fourth of July Trailhead, take the Arapaho Pass trail past the Diamond Lake junction (about 1.1 mi) to the Fourth of July Mine ruins (about 2 mi). Turn sharply back to the northeast onto the signed Arapaho Glacier trail and follow it above treeline to the saddle between the peaks' southeast shoulder (about 12,700 ft), then scramble to South Arapaho's summit (about 4.3 mi from the trailhead).
routes.descent_text: Reverse the traverse south to South Arapaho, then descend the Arapaho Glacier trail and Arapaho Pass trail back to the trailhead. Descending the east side of the ridge toward the glacier is not an option: that basin is closed to all entry.
routes.turnaround: Be off the ridge and heading back from South Arapaho by early afternoon at the latest; turn around at the first sign of building thunderstorms, since the traverse takes an hour or more each way with no quick way down.
routes.bail: Before the traverse, South Arapaho's summit is the natural turnaround. On the ridge, the only safe retreat is back the way you came to South Arapaho; do not try to descend east toward the glacier, which is steep, loose and closed to entry.

pitch_detail.notes: Arapaho Pass trail to the mine ruins, Arapaho Glacier trail to the saddle, then a loose rocky scramble past a false summit to the top.
Leave South Arapaho northward; an exposed downclimb of about 50 ft, then sustained blocky scrambling. Stay near the crest, escape west at difficulties.
About three quarters of the way along: two short steps of roughly 8-10 ft each on good holds, above exposure.
Easier ground, sometimes a snow patch, to the broad summit.
Reverse the ridge back to South Arapaho; the crux steps are downclimbed.
Scramble off South Arapaho and follow the trails back down.

what_to_bring: Plenty of water; little is available above the mine ruins
Snacks for a long day above treeline
obj_haz: Afternoon thunderstorms on a long, exposed ridge
Loose rock and rockfall from parties above
Steep drop-offs on the glacier side
routes.watch_out:
The Arapaho Glacier basin east of the ridge is Boulder's watershed and closed to all entry
The crux steps must be downclimbed on the way back
Route markings on the ridge are sparse
pro_tips: Start before dawn; the lot fills very early on summer weekends
Stay on or just west of the crest when in doubt
Budget at least two hours round trip for the ridge alone
Keep an eye on the sky from South Arapaho before committing to the ridge

road.name: Fourth of July Road (County Road 111) from Eldora
road.status: Seasonal; not plowed, typically drivable roughly late spring through early fall
road.driveNote: From Nederland take County Road 130 west through Eldora. The pavement ends past town; keep right at the fork onto the Fourth of July road for about 4-5 miles of rough, rocky dirt to the lot by Buckingham Campground. Passable for careful passenger cars in summer, but higher clearance helps. Parking is limited and fills very early on summer weekends; never block the road or private drives.

access.land_manager: Arapaho and Roosevelt National Forests (Indian Peaks Wilderness)
access.permit: No permit or timed entry for day use; an overnight wilderness permit is required from June 1 to September 15
